Personally, I run /tmp as tmpfs these days, which is just a ram drive. For swap, I run 2GB across the board, on everything I build, regardless of the size, because if you're swapping, then you need to add ram -- I just keep it around so the box doesn't crash in the event of a ram overflow, and so I'll know that I need to... you guessed it: add ram.

As for /var and /home, it's really dealer's choice. In server environments, I break out /var/log and /var/log/audit so I don't fill filesystems up, but that's not really a concern for a desktop system. If I were you, I'd forego the idea of partitioning the HDD entirely, cp -rp the contents of /var and /home to the hdd, mv the directories to a different name, and then symlink them to their new location on the HDD. what are the concerns here in the event of a crash...

Since both ramfs and tmpfs is writing to the system RAM, it would get deleted once the system gets rebooted, or crashed. So, you should write a process to pick up the data from ramfs/tmpfs to disk in periodic intervals. You can also write a process to write down the data from ramfs/tmpfs to disk while the system is shutting down. But, this will not help you in the time of system crash.

obviously i would lose /tmp on shutdown, but why is this a concern on a crash?

do you dump this data to disk periodically on your boxes?

No, /tmp is basically stuff that can be safely lost. Caches, one time things. Even if you have your tmp on disks, it is erased every boot up (or on boot down, dont remember). Things that are temporary, that can safely be lost but is nice to not loose are stored in /var/tmp.

What the author is talking about is using tmpfs for stuff that should not be lost. For instance, if you mount /var/log in a tmpfs, then you would lose the system logs on a crash. Losing logs is not the end of the world, but it is nice to have them when you try to fix things.

One more thing that just ocurred to me and can be a source of confusion: tmpfs is not the same thing as /tmp.

tmpfs is a filesystem that takes a chunck of memory and makes it look like a disk, with files and folders. You could mount anything in a tmpfs, if you need to.

/tmp is a point on your directory tree. It is a place that the system uses specifically for stuff that are temporary and the system knows that can be lost.

5 GB for /tmp??? Where did you saw this recomendation??? That is wayyyy to much. Mine has only 100M and it is never more than 30% used. Right now it uses only 20K. Do you have a special need for such a big /tmp? Are you planning in using any software that throws huge files at /tmp?

But anyway, you can mount a huge tmpfs that you will not lose RAM, because the system will only use what it needs. If you only have 50M of actual data stored in a tmpfs, that is the actual ram it will use. Mounting with 5GB is only telling the system the maximum allowed size. It means the system will allow it to grow when there is need, consuming the RAM, up to 5GB. If you look at the filesystem size, it will report as 5GB, but if you look at the memory use, only the de facto used memory is reserved.

You could do either, if you're so inclined; the installer's partition manager is pretty good about telling you if something won't work. Alternatively, you could just do a vanilla install and manage it all after the fact -- I prefer this route because it disturbs my calm when the installer craps all over itself and I have to start over.

Basically, if you want to manage the HDD after a clean install on the SSD, you'll want to add the HDD to a new volume group (become familiar with LVM), create however many logical volumes, sized and named appropriately, you want, then format the logical volumes as if they were physical drives. You'll want to become familiar with the fstab, and always remember to test your mount entries before you reboot, else you'll be booting into single user to fix things. The only tricky thing is that you'll need to mount your partitions, say data-vg_home-lv, somewhere other than their final destination in order to grab the data, say /mnt. So you would mount /dev/mapper/data-vg_home-lv /mnt then cp -rp /home/* /mnt then umount /mnt then mv /home /home_old then mkdir /home then mount /dev/mapper/data-vg_home-lv /home... or something similar. Then just add your entries to fstab and test them.

The fun bit is learning LVM; once you have that down, you're golden.

I would partition it like this.

  • /boot = 4 GB
  • / = 30 GB
  • SWAP = 6GB
  • unpartitioned = 30 GB
  • /home = the rest (430 GB in this case)

The reason for the 30 gig unpartitioned is that it when it comes time to do a dist-upgrade or you want to try a different distro, you would install it there. Leave /boot and /home untouched when doing the install. When the install is done, you will be dual booting with two different versions so that way if you don't like the new version or something broke with an update, you can just boot off the old version and recover everything.

I know I'm gonna sound condescending, but if you're new to Linux, just install using root and swap. It will be easier for you to navigate until you get your bearings and decide that you actually need /var and /usr and /tmp and boot in vfat and btrfs partition and whatnot. Making a bunch of partitions won't do shit for your SSD, mostly because you will never write so much data how much the modern SSD can endure, not in any scenario. Second, making a bunch of partitions will require you to install via UEFI and rEFInd, which are basically synonymes for anal sex if you're new and fresh in Linux land, and especially on a distro like Mint that is preconfigured to run everything for you yet falls face down and shits itself the moment you have to configure it manually.

TL:DR If you're not ready to go balls deep with a distro that requires you to configure pretty much everything like Arch and Gentoo, then you don't want to fuck around with all those partitions. It's mostly pointless since you won't be cloning your drive or making system rescue any time soon and you can use your other hard drive to backup data for reinstalling.

P.S. Just use ext4, it's been around for a while and it's stable enough.
